questions.stem: Consider the control flow graph given below. Which one of the following options is the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?
questions.figure: Control flow graph with ENTRY, EXIT and four blocks. ENTRY goes to B1 (a = b + c). B1 has two successors: B2 (d = a + e) and B3 (e = a + f). B2 goes to B4 (g = d + e). B4 goes to EXIT. B3 has a back edge to B1.

diagram.alt: Flow graph: ENTRY, B1 with a = b + c, B1 to B2 (d = a + e) and to B3 (e = a + f), B2 to B4 (g = d + e), B4 to EXIT, B3 back to B1.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same flow graph with the live-out set written beside each block: B1 {a,b,c,e,f}, B2 {d,e}, B3 {b,c,e,f}, B4 empty.

steps.title: What live means, and the backward rule
steps.body: A variable is live at a point if some path from that point reads it before writing it. The live-out set of a block is everything live just after its last instruction. Two sets per block drive the calculation: use (variables read before any write inside the block) and def (variables written in the block). The rule is backward: in(B) = use(B) union (out(B) minus def(B)), and out(B) is the union of in(S) over every successor S of B. Nothing is live after the last block, because the program ends. Start from B4 and walk against the edges.

steps.title: Write use and def for each block
steps.body: B1 (a = b + c): use {b, c}, def {a}. B2 (d = a + e): use {a, e}, def {d}. B3 (e = a + f): use {a, f}, def {e}. B4 (g = d + e): use {d, e}, def {g}. A name on the left is written, names on the right are read, and each block has one instruction, so there is no read-before-write ordering to worry about.

steps.title: Blocks without the loop
steps.body: B4 leaves the program, so out(B4) = ∅ and in(B4) = {d, e}. B2 has only B4 after it, so out(B2) = in(B4) = {d, e}. Then in(B2) = {a, e} ∪ ({d, e} − {d}) = {a, e}.

steps.title: The loop B1, B3 forces an iteration
steps.body: out(B1) = in(B2) ∪ in(B3) and out(B3) = in(B1). Start with out(B3) = ∅. Then in(B3) = {a, f}, so out(B1) = {a, e} ∪ {a, f} = {a, e, f}, and in(B1) = {b, c} ∪ ({a, e, f} − {a}) = {b, c, e, f}. Now out(B3) = {b, c, e, f}, so in(B3) = {a, f} ∪ ({b, c, e, f} − {e}) = {a, b, c, f}. Redo out(B1) = {a, e} ∪ {a, b, c, f} = {a, b, c, e, f}, and in(B1) is still {b, c, e, f} (a is defined in B1). Nothing changes on the next round, so this is the fixed point.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The set for B1, B2, B3 and B4 is {a,b,c,e,f}, {d,e}, {b,c,e,f}, ∅, which is option A.

shortcut.body: B4 must be empty and B2 must be {d, e}: that is already true in A, B and C. B1 has successors that read a, e and f, so out(B1) cannot be empty: that removes B and D. A and C differ at B3, where out(B3) = in(B1), and B1 reads b and c, which nothing in B1 or B3 writes, so b must be live out of B3. Only A has b there. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Taking out(B1) as empty or out(B3) as {a, c, f} reads the use sets as live-out. use(B3) is what B3 needs before it runs, not what is live after it.
out(B3) = {c, e, f} drops b. b is read by B1 on the next trip around the loop, and B3 does not write b, so b is live out of B3.

Putting f into out(B2) takes it from B3's use set, but B3 is not a successor of B2: B2's only successor is B4, which reads d and e only. An empty out(B1) is also wrong, because B2 and B3 read a, e and f. Adding a to out(B3) ignores that B1 redefines a before reading it.
Stopping after one pass over the loop gives out(B3) = ∅ or {a, e, f}. The back edge B3 to B1 needs a second pass until no set changes.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the set of live variables at the exit of every basic block of a flow graph with single-assignment blocks and a back edge from B3 to B1.
recognize.contrast: Available expressions also solve equations over a flow graph, but they run forward and meet by intersection. Live variables run backward and meet by union, and the question here asks what is read later, not what was computed earlier.

check.body: Track one variable end to end. f is read in B3 and written nowhere, so it is live on every edge from which B3 can still be reached. B3 is reachable from the exits of B1 and of B3 itself through the loop, but not from the exits of B2 or B4, so f belongs in exactly the first two sets.

hints.text: What does it mean for a variable to be live just after a block, and in which direction through the graph does that information travel?
A variable is live at a point if some path from there reads it before overwriting it. A value nobody will read again does not need to be kept.

Work backward. What is live after a block is the union of what is live at the start of each successor, and what is live at the start of a block is what it reads plus what is live after it minus what it writes.

For each block list the variables it reads and the one it writes. Begin at the block that leaves the graph, where nothing is live, and move against the edges. A back edge feeds a later block into an earlier one, so some sets may need a second look.
B4 has no successor, so nothing is live after it. It reads d and e, so both are live at its entry.

variation.stem: A flow graph has blocks B1 to B4, each with one instruction. B1: a = b + c. B2: d = a * e. B3: e = d + f. B4: g = e + a. The edges are B1 to B2, B2 to B3, B2 to B4, B3 to B2, and B4 leaves the graph. Which option gives the live variables at the exit of B1, B2, B3 and B4, in that order?
variation.explanation: Use in(B) = use(B) union (out(B) minus def(B)) and out(B) = union of in over successors, working backward. The loop B2, B3 needs a second pass: the first pass leaves out(B3) empty, and the second gives out(B3) = in(B2) = {a, e, f}. Then out(B2) = in(B3) union in(B4) = {d, f, a, e}. Option B lists read sets, option C forgets that B4 reads a, and option D stops after one pass.

questions.stem: Consider the control flow graph shown in the figure. Which one of the following options correctly lists the set of redundant expressions (common subexpressions) in the basic blocks B4 and B5? Note: All the variables are integers.
questions.figure: Control flow graph. ENTRY goes to B1 (a = b + i). B1 goes to B2 and to B3. B2 contains, in order, a = g * k; f = d - f; a = c * 4. B3 contains, in order, t = g * k; b = c + m. B2 and B3 both go to B4 (x = g * k; y = b + i). B4 goes to B5 (z = c + m). B5 goes to EXIT.

diagram.alt: Flow graph: B1 a = b + i branches to B2 (a = g*k, f = d - f, a = c*4) and B3 (t = g*k, b = c + m); both join at B4 (x = g*k, y = b + i), then B5 (z = c + m).

solutionDiagram.alt: The same graph annotated: g*k is available out of both B2 and B3, b+i is killed on the B3 path, c+m is missing on the B2 path, so only g*k in B4 is redundant.

steps.title: What a redundant expression is
steps.body: An expression such as g * k is redundant at a point if, on every path from ENTRY to that point, it has already been computed and neither g nor k has been assigned since. Such an expression is called available. A computation of an available expression can be replaced by the earlier result. Two events matter: gen (the expression is computed) and kill (an operand is assigned). The meeting rule at a join is intersection, since the expression must be available on all incoming paths.

steps.title: Available at the end of B2 and B3
steps.body: B1: computes b + i, kills nothing that matters. End of B1: {b + i}. B2: a = g * k adds g * k; f = d - f changes only f; a = c * 4 changes only a, and a is not an operand of any expression here. End of B2: {b + i, g * k}. B3: t = g * k adds g * k; b = c + m adds c + m and then kills b + i because b is assigned. End of B3: {g * k, c + m}.

steps.title: Join into B4 and check B4
steps.body: The intersection of {b + i, g * k} and {g * k, c + m} is {g * k}. So g * k is available at the start of B4 and the instruction x = g * k recomputes it: redundant. b + i is not available (B3 killed it), so y = b + i is not redundant. Redundant in B4: {g * k}.

steps.title: Check B5
steps.body: B4 adds nothing new that matters for c + m (x = g * k and y = b + i do not compute it and assign only x and y). c + m was computed only on the B3 path, so it is not in the intersection and z = c + m is not redundant. Redundant in B5: { }. The answer is option D.

shortcut.body: Ask of each repeated expression: is it computed on both branches before the join, with its operands untouched? g * k is computed in both B2 and B3, so B4 has it. b + i is computed only before the split and b is rewritten in B3. c + m appears only in B3. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Marking b + i redundant because B1 computed it ignores that b = c + m in B3 changes b on one path. A single path that kills an expression stops it being available at the join.
Marking c + m redundant in B5 uses the B3 path alone. It was computed only there; the path through B2 reaches B5 without it.
Listing g * k and b + i together is the same b + i mistake, with the right g * k added.
Believing a = c * 4 in B2 kills g * k because a was assigned from g * k first. Only an assignment to g or k kills g * k.

recognize.clues: The question asks for redundant expressions (common subexpressions) in blocks that follow a branch and a join, with operands reassigned on one of the branches.
recognize.contrast: Live variables also run on this kind of graph, but they go backward and union at joins. Redundancy needs the forward analysis with intersection at the join.

check.body: Test the weakest path for each candidate. For b + i, take B1, B3, B4: b is assigned in B3 after b + i was computed, so B4 must compute it afresh. For c + m, take B1, B2, B4, B5: nothing on that path computes c + m, so B5 must compute it. g * k has no such failing path, because both B2 and B3 compute it and neither changes g or k afterwards.

hints.text: For each of the two blocks, which right-hand sides were already computed on every route that reaches it, with no operand changed since?
An expression is available at a point if every path to that point has computed it and none of its operands has been reassigned afterwards. Computing an available expression again is redundant.
At a join the available sets coming in are intersected, not united, because the old value must exist whichever way control arrived. An assignment to an operand removes every expression that uses it.

Walk each branch from its start to its end, adding what is computed and dropping what an assignment spoils. Combine the two branch ends at the join, then walk the join block and the block after it with the same rules.
After B1 the expression b + i is available. B3 then assigns b. Ask what that assignment does to b + i at the end of B3.

variation.stem: Consider this flow graph. B1: t = a + b. B1 goes to B2 and to B3. B2: p = a * b; c = c + 1. B3: q = a * b; d = e + f. Both B2 and B3 go to B4: r = a * b; s = c + 1. B4 goes to B5: u = e + f; v = c + 1. All variables are integers. Which option lists the redundant expressions in B4 and then in B5?
variation.explanation: B2 ends with a * b available (c = c + 1 computes c + 1 and then spoils it by assigning c). B3 ends with a * b and e + f available. The intersection at B4 is { a * b }, so only r = a * b is redundant, and s = c + 1 then makes c + 1 available. At B5, e + f was computed on only one branch, so u is not redundant, but v = c + 1 is.

questions.stem: Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions SDD1 and SDD2 for type declarations. D is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal V1 is the same as V and the non-terminal D1 is the same as D. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier. Let P and Q be the languages specified by grammars G1 and G2, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: The languages P and Q are the same
SDD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes
SDD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes
The specifications of SDD1 and SDD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

steps.title: The terms
steps.body: A syntax-directed definition (SDD) attaches a rule to each production that computes attributes. An attribute of a node is synthesized if its rule sits in a production whose head is that node and reads the node's children. It is inherited if the rule is in the parent's production and sets a child's attribute from the parent or siblings. An SDD is S-attributed if it has only synthesized attributes, and L-attributed if every inherited attribute depends only on the parent's inherited attributes and symbols to the left. Every S-attributed SDD is L-attributed. Check each statement against these definitions, and against the grammars for the language question.

steps.title: Statement A: the languages
steps.body: G1: D → T V, V → V id | id gives a type word followed by one or more ids: (int | float) id+. G2: D → D id | T id unrolls to T id id*, which is the same set of strings. So P = Q and statement A is true.

steps.title: Statement B: SDD2
steps.body: In D → D1 id the rule sets D.type from D1.type, a child. In D → T id, D.type comes from T.type. T.type is set from a constant. The put calls only update the table and set no attribute. Every attribute is synthesized, so SDD2 is S-attributed. B is true.

steps.title: Statement C: SDD1
steps.body: V.type and V1.type are inherited (set from the parent T or V). But T.type is set by T → int and T → float from the production's own head, which is synthesized, and D.type is synthesized too. SDD1 has both kinds, so 'only inherited' is false. C is false.

steps.title: Statement D: the table entries
steps.body: In SDD1 the type travels from T down to V and then to each id, so each id gets the type of T through put(id.entry, V.type). In SDD2 the type travels up through D and each id gets put(id.entry, D1.type) or put(id.entry, T.type), which is the same T type. For a declaration such as int a b c both put the pair (a, int), (b, int), (c, int). D is true. The correct set is A, B, D.

shortcut.body: Statement C is the easy one to kill: T → int sets T.type from a constant, which cannot be inherited, so SDD1 has a synthesized attribute. Then confirm A by writing the two languages as (int|float) id+ and B by noting that SDD2 has no rule that assigns to a right-hand-side symbol. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Reading 'V.type = T.type' as the only kind of rule in SDD1 and calling the whole SDD inherited. T.type = int is synthesized, so the SDD has both kinds.
Dropping A because G1 and G2 look different. They differ in the derivation tree (right recursion through V versus left recursion through D) but generate the same strings.
Dropping D because put appears in a different production in each SDD. What matters is what is stored: the same (id, type) pair per identifier.

recognize.clues: Two syntax-directed definitions are given as tables of rules, and the statements ask whether each is S-attributed, L-attributed or has only inherited attributes, and what it does to the symbol table.
recognize.contrast: The language question (statement about P and Q) is decided by the grammars alone, with no regard to the rules. The attribute questions are decided by the rules alone, so keep the two kinds apart.

check.body: Run one concrete string through both definitions. For float x y, both grammars derive it, and under each the put calls record x with float and y with float, so the two symbol tables agree. Then list every attribute assigned in SDD2 and note whether its rule names a head or a body symbol; a lone body-symbol assignment would change the classification.

hints.text: For each statement, which definition does it lean on: the strings a grammar derives, where each rule writes its result, or which neighbours a rule reads?
An attribute is synthesized when its rule sits in the production of its own node and reads the children. It is inherited when the rule sets a child attribute from the parent or from siblings.

S-attributed means every attribute is synthesized. L-attributed allows inherited attributes only if each reads the parent inherited attributes or symbols to its left. Every S-attributed definition passes the L-attributed test.

For the language statement, unroll each grammar into a pattern over int, float and id. For the attribute statements, list what each rule assigns and mark it head or body symbol. For the table statement, trace the put calls for one sample declaration under each definition.
Take the declaration int a b. List the put calls SDD1 makes, with the type value each call receives.

variation.stem: An SDD for an expression grammar has these productions and rules. E → T R { R.i = T.val; E.val = R.s }. R → + T R1 { R1.i = R.i + T.val; R.s = R1.s }. R → ε { R.s = R.i }. T → num { T.val = num.lexval }. Which of the following statements is/are true?
variation.explanation: R.i is inherited because the rules assign it to the body symbols R and R1, and R.s, E.val and T.val are written on the head, so they are synthesized. Having an inherited attribute rules out S-attributed. Each inherited rule reads only T.val (to the left of R) or R.i (the head inherited attribute), so the SDD is L-attributed.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for intermediate code generation: (I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass. (II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass. Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?

steps.title: The problem backpatching solves
steps.body: Three-address code uses jumps such as 'if x < y goto L'. When the compiler emits a jump out of a Boolean test, the target label may be a statement not yet generated, for example the code after an else branch. Two-pass schemes leave the label blank and fill it in on a second walk. Backpatching does the same in one pass: it keeps a list of the jump instructions whose targets are unknown (a truelist and a falselist) and fills in the label for the whole list the moment the target address is known.

steps.title: Boolean expressions
steps.body: For B → B1 || B2, the false-exits of B1 are patched to the start of B2, and the true-exits of both join the truelist of B. For B → B1 && B2 the true-exits of B1 are patched to the start of B2. The compiler records the start of B2 with a marker nonterminal while parsing, in a single bottom-up pass. So statement (I) is correct.

steps.title: Flow-of-control statements
steps.body: For S → if (B) S1 else S2 and S → while (B) S1, the true-exits of B are patched to the start of S1 and the false-exits to the code after the statement or to the else part. The list of unfilled exits of a statement is passed upward as its nextlist and patched when the next statement is reached. This is the same mechanism, so (II) is also correct. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: Backpatching exists precisely to generate jump code for Booleans and control flow without a second pass (Aho et al. section 6.7). If the options say it fails on either one, the option is wrong. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Thinking backpatching is only for Booleans because truelist and falselist are introduced there. The same lists, with nextlist, drive if, if-else, while and sequences of statements.
Thinking Boolean expressions need a separate pass because they are 'values'. In jumping code a Boolean is compiled into jumps, and those jumps are exactly what get backpatched.
Remembering only that backpatching 'leaves holes'. Leaving a hole and filling it in the same pass is what keeps the translation one pass.

recognize.clues: The words backpatching, one pass, Boolean expression and flow-of-control point to jump code whose targets are filled in from truelist and falselist style lists.
recognize.contrast: Resolving labels in a second pass also fills in jump targets, but it walks the code twice. Backpatching fills them in the same pass, as soon as each target address becomes known.

check.body: Try while (x < y) z = 1 as a sample. The test creates a true exit and a false exit, and the body ends with a jump back. The true exit is patched once the body start is known and the false exit once the code after the loop begins, all during one pass. A Boolean expression such as a < b || c < d alone needs the same lists, so both constructs fit.

hints.text: When code for a Boolean test or a loop is produced in one left-to-right pass, what is not yet known about some jump instructions at the moment they are written?
A jump may need a target that is generated later. Backpatching records such incomplete jumps in lists and fills in their targets once the address is known.

The lists of unfinished jumps (true exits, false exits, next exits) are merged as the parse moves up the tree, and a marker captures an instruction address when needed. That is how a second pass is avoided.

Judge the two statements one at a time. For each, name the jumps its construct creates, ask whether their targets are known when they are emitted, and ask whether the list mechanism can supply them later. Then combine the two verdicts.

variation.stem: A one-pass compiler uses backpatching on if (a < b && c < d) x = 1; Each relational test produces two instructions, a conditional jump then an unconditional jump, so the four jumps sit at addresses 100 to 103. The assignment x = 1 is at 104, and the next statement starts at 105. Which option gives the final targets of the jumps at 100, 101, 102 and 103, in that order?
variation.explanation: The true exit of the first test (100) is patched to the start of the second test, 102. The true exit of the second test (102) is patched to the start of the body, 104. Both false exits (101 and 103) stay on the false list and are patched to 105 when the next statement begins. Option A skips the second test, option B sends the false exit of the first test (101) into the second test, which is what || does for a false exit of its first operand, and option D sends a false exit into the body.

questions.stem: Given the following syntax directed translation rules: Rule 1: R → A B {B.i = R.i − 1; A.i = B.i; R.i = A.i + 1;}. Rule 2: P → C D {P.i = C.i + D.i; D.i = C.i + 2;}. Rule 3: Q → E F {Q.i = E.i + F.i;}. Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?
options: Rule 1 is S-attributed and L-attributed; Rule 2 is S-attributed and not L-attributed; Rule 3 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed
Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed; Rule 2 is S-attributed and L-attributed; Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed
Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed; Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed; Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed
Rule 1 is S-attributed and not L-attributed; Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed; Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: In a production X → Y1 Y2, a rule that assigns to the head X computes a synthesized attribute. A rule that assigns to a body symbol Yk computes an inherited attribute of Yk. An SDD is S-attributed if every rule is synthesized. It is L-attributed if every inherited rule for Yk reads only the head's inherited attributes and attributes of symbols to the left of Yk (and its own). All attributes here are named i, and which kind each is depends on where the rule writes.

steps.title: Rule 3
steps.body: Q.i = E.i + F.i assigns to the head, so it is synthesized, and no rule writes to E or F. Rule 3 is S-attributed, and therefore L-attributed too.

steps.title: Rule 2
steps.body: P.i = C.i + D.i is synthesized. D.i = C.i + 2 writes to the body symbol D, so D.i is inherited, and it reads C, which is to the left of D. That keeps the rule L-attributed. An inherited rule means it is not S-attributed. Rule 2: not S-attributed, L-attributed.

steps.title: Rule 1
steps.body: A.i = B.i writes to A and reads B, which is to the right of A. An inherited attribute may not depend on a symbol to its right, so Rule 1 is not L-attributed, and since it has inherited rules it is not S-attributed. (B.i = R.i − 1 is fine, it reads the head. A.i = B.i is the failing rule. R.i = A.i + 1 is synthesized.) Rule 1: neither. The answer is option C.

shortcut.body: Find the rules that write to a body symbol (inherited). If there is none: S-attributed, hence L-attributed. If there is one, look at its right side for a symbol to the right of the target or a synthesized attribute of the head. A.i = B.i points right, so Rule 1 fails both tests. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Calling Rule 1 S- and L-attributed and Rule 3 neither gets both verdicts backwards: Rule 3 only writes to its head Q, so it is S-attributed, while Rule 1 writes to the body symbols B and A. S-attributed is decided by where the rule writes, not by the shared attribute name i.
Calling Rule 2 S-attributed because P.i is synthesized. D.i = C.i + 2 is a second rule in the same production and writes to a body symbol.
Calling Rule 1 S-attributed because it ends with R.i = A.i + 1. The first two rules write to B and A, so they are inherited, and A.i = B.i also reads a right sibling.

recognize.clues: Each rule assigns attributes named i to both heads and body symbols, and the options ask for S-attributed and L-attributed per rule.
recognize.contrast: S-attributed is stricter than L-attributed. Every S-attributed rule is also L-attributed, while an L-attributed rule is S-attributed only when it has no inherited assignment.

check.body: Check Rule 1 by dependency order. A.i needs B.i, and B.i needs R.i, so B.i must be computed before A.i, yet a left-to-right pass reaches A first. That ordering conflict confirms the position rule by an independent route. In Rule 2, D.i needs only C.i, which is visited first, so no conflict arises.

hints.text: For each rule, does every assignment write to the head of the production or to a symbol in its body?
A rule that writes to the head defines a synthesized attribute. A rule that writes to a body symbol defines an inherited attribute of that symbol.
S-attributed needs every rule to be synthesized. L-attributed lets an inherited attribute read only the head attributes and the symbols to its left in the body.
Go rule by rule. List each assignment and mark it synthesized or inherited. For each inherited one, mark where every symbol it reads sits relative to the symbol being written.
Rule 3 has a single assignment, and it writes to a head, so it is synthesized. Ask whether a rule with head assignments only leaves anything for a left-to-right test to check.

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?

steps.title: What live variable analysis tells you
steps.body: A variable is live at a point if its current value may still be read later on some path. Live variable analysis computes, for each point, the set of live variables. A variable that is not live has a value no one will read, so the machine can reuse whatever holds it.

steps.title: Which technique needs that answer
steps.body: Register assignment (allocation) has to decide which variables share a limited number of registers. Two variables can share a register exactly when they are never live at the same time. So the interference graph used for register allocation is built from live ranges, which come from live variable analysis.

steps.title: Why the others do not
steps.body: Strength reduction replaces an expensive operation by a cheaper one (x * 2 by x + x), and only needs to look at the expression and loop structure. Constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time. Run-time function call management concerns activation records and linkage. None of these asks whether a value is read later. The answer is option B.

shortcut.body: Live variables is the register-allocation analysis; the other usual users are dead code elimination and spill decisions. If an option says registers, take it. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Run-time call management sounds related to storage but it handles stack frames, not whether a value will be used again.
Strength reduction is a loop optimization built on induction variables, a different analysis from liveness.
Constant folding needs constant propagation (which values are known), not which values are still needed.

recognize.clues: The stem names live variable analysis and the options list compiler techniques, so the question is which technique consumes liveness information.
recognize.contrast: Available expressions, used to remove repeated computations, is a different forward analysis. Dead code elimination also uses liveness, but it is not among the choices.

check.body: Take straight-line code with two temporaries whose lifetimes do not overlap. Liveness shows they can share one register. Constant folding on the same code needs no lifetime facts, only the operand values, and strength reduction needs only the form of each instruction.

questions.stem: Refer to the given 3-address code sequence. This code sequence is split into basic blocks. The number of basic blocks is ________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: The listing cut into six boxes: 1001; 1002; 1003 to 1009; 1010 to 1011; 1012; 1013 to 1017.

steps.title: Basic block and leader
steps.body: A basic block is a maximal run of instructions that runs from its first instruction to its last with no jump into the middle and no jump out except at the end. The first instruction of each block is a leader. The rules: (1) the first instruction of the program is a leader; (2) the target of any jump is a leader; (3) the instruction right after a jump is a leader. Each leader starts one block, which runs until the next leader.

steps.title: Apply the three rules
steps.body: Rule 1: 1001. Rule 2: the targets are 1003 (from 1009), 1002 (from 1011) and 1013 (from 1017). Rule 3: the instructions after the jumps at 1009, 1011 and 1017 are 1010, 1012 and 1018. There is no 1018, so it adds nothing. The leaders are 1001, 1002, 1003, 1010, 1012, 1013.

steps.title: Cut and count
steps.body: Blocks: 1001 alone; 1002 alone; 1003 to 1009; 1010 to 1011; 1012 alone; 1013 to 1017. That is 6 blocks. The answer is 6.

shortcut.body: Count the distinct leaders: one for the start, one per distinct jump target, one per instruction after a jump, merging coincidences. Here 1 + 3 targets + 2 after-jump (1010, 1012) = 6, since 1002 and 1003 are different targets. About 1 minute.

traps.text: 5: forgetting that 1002 is a target of the jump at 1011, so it starts its own block apart from 1001.
7: counting the position after the last jump 1017 as a leader. There is no instruction there.
4 or 3: cutting only at the jumps (3 jump instructions), instead of using targets and the instruction after each jump as well.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the number of basic blocks in a numbered three-address listing that contains conditional jumps of the form if ... goto.
recognize.contrast: Counting jumps plus one is not the rule. A jump target and the instruction after a jump each start a block, and one instruction can be both, so the leaders must be merged before counting.

check.body: Write the six address ranges and test them. They must tile 1001 to 1017 with no gap or overlap, every jump must be the last instruction of its range, and every jump target must be the first instruction of its range. If any test failed, a leader would be missing.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects
The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth-first order
Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed
All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammar can be evaluated using a bottom-up parsing strategy

steps.title: The facts to hold
steps.body: An SDD attaches semantic rules to productions. In an attribute grammar the rules are functions with no side effects (as opposed to an SDT, which may run actions). A synthesized attribute reads children only. An L-attributed SDD lets an inherited attribute read the parent's inherited attributes and left siblings. Judge each statement for truth, and pick the false ones.

steps.title: A and C are true
steps.body: A is the textbook definition of an attribute grammar: no side effects. C is true: when a bottom-up parser reduces by A → X1 … Xn, the children's attribute values are on the stack, so the head's synthesized attribute is computed at the reduction.

steps.title: B is false
steps.body: L-attributed means exactly that a single left-to-right depth-first traversal can evaluate all attributes: visit the children in order, computing each child's inherited attributes just before entering it and the head's synthesized attributes at the end. So they can always be evaluated in depth-first order. The statement says they cannot always be, which is false.

steps.title: D is false
steps.body: The guarantee for bottom-up evaluation of L-attributed SDDs (Aho et al. 5.5) holds when the grammar is LL(1): then the SDD can be converted into an SDT and evaluated with a bottom-up parser by adding markers and copying inherited values on the stack. For a general LR(1) grammar the markers can introduce conflicts, so the claim 'all' is false. The false statements are B and D.

shortcut.body: Know two stock facts: L-attributed always means a left-to-right depth-first pass exists (so B is false); and the 'any L-attributed SDD can go bottom-up' theorem needs an LL grammar, not LR(1) (so D is false). About 1 minute.

traps.text: Marking A false because an SDT has side effects. The question is about the attribute grammar, whose rules are side-effect free.
Marking C false because bottom-up parsers are thought to handle only inherited attributes badly. Synthesized attributes are exactly what the bottom-up parser handles well.
Letting D pass because LR(1) is more powerful than LL(1). The transformation needs marker nonterminals, which can break the LR property.

recognize.clues: Four statements about attribute grammars, L-attributed definitions, synthesized attributes and parsing strategy, with the stem asking for the FALSE ones.
recognize.contrast: An attribute grammar has rules without side effects, while a syntax-directed translation scheme embeds actions that may have side effects. The first statement is about the former.

check.body: Test statement B on a small rule. For A → X Y with Y.i = X.s, a left-to-right depth-first walk visits X, learns X.s, then sets Y.i before entering Y, so it works. A rule X.i = Y.s reads from the right and is not L-attributed, so it is outside what the statement is about. Every L-attributed rule behaves like the first case.

questions.stem: Consider the following expression: x[i] = (p + r) * -s[i] + u/w. The following sequence shows the list of triples representing the given expression, with entries missing for triples (1), (3), and (6). Which one of the following options fills in the missing entries CORRECTLY?

solutionDiagram.alt: Expression tree with each operator labelled by its triple number: (0) p + r, (1) s[i] read, (2) uminus, (3) multiply, (4) u / w, (5) add, (6) x[i] address, (7) assignment.

steps.title: Triples and the two array operators
steps.body: A triple has one operator and two operands, and it has no result name: a later triple refers to it by its number, such as (2). Arrays use two operators. =[] with operands (a, i) reads a[i] and its value can be used by later triples. []= with operands (a, i) names the element a[i] as a target, and a following = triple stores the value into it.

steps.title: Evaluate in operator order
steps.body: Triples appear in the order operations happen. (0) + p r is p + r. The operand -s[i] needs s[i] first: (1) =[] s i. Then (2) uminus (1) negates it. The product of (p + r) with -s[i] is (3) * (0) (2). (4) / u w and (5) + (3) (4) complete the right side.

steps.title: The left side
steps.body: x[i] on the left of = is a target. (6) []= x i names that element. (7) = (6) (5) then stores triple (5) into the element named by (6). So (1) =[] s i, (3) * (0) (2), (6) []= x i, option A.

steps.title: Rule out the others
steps.body: B and D use a minus sign in (3), but the expression multiplies by a negated value; the minus is already done by uminus in (2). B and D also use []= to read s[i], which reads and writes the wrong way round. C has the correct (1) and (3) but gives (6) the operand (5): that would put the value into the operand slot of the target, and (7) already refers to (5) itself.

shortcut.body: Three eliminations. Operator (3) must be *, because the expression is (p + r) * (-s[i]); that kills B and D. Then (6) is the target x[i], whose operands are x and i, not a value: that kills C. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Reading the uminus as a binary minus and using - for (3), and swapping the two array operators.
Putting (5) into the operand of x[i]. The address operand of []= is the index i; the value (5) is supplied by the = in (7).
Reading the array on the right with []= instead of =[]. The read operator is =[].

recognize.clues: The table gives triples with operands written as row numbers such as (1) and (4), and two array operators whose roles the question hides.
recognize.contrast: Quadruples name a result in each row, so rows can be reordered; triples refer to results by row number, which is why the order of the rows here is forced.

check.body: Read the finished table back as an expression. Row (3) multiplies the sum p + r by the negated s[i]; row (5) adds u/w; row (7) stores that value into the element that row (6) names. Every row number mentioned as an operand must point to an earlier row, and in the correct choice each one does.

questions.stem: Consider the following syntax-directed definition (SDD). Given "MMLK" as the input, which one of the following options is the CORRECT value computed by the SDD (in the attribute S.val)?

steps.title: What to compute
steps.body: The input is split by the grammar into D H T U in order. Every rule here computes val from the children's val, so it is a synthesized definition: value flows from the leaves up to S. The strings: D takes the leading Ms, H takes the Ls, T the Cs, and U the K. Process each letter-group on its own and add.

steps.title: Split MMLK
steps.body: M M go to D, L goes to H, T has no C so it derives ε, and K goes to U.

steps.title: Compute each part
steps.body: D: two Ms then ε: D.val = 5 + (5 + (−5)) = 5. H: one L then ε: H.val = 50 + (−10) = 40. T: ε only, so T.val = −5. U: U.val = 5.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: S.val = 45, which is option A.

shortcut.body: Each letter adds its weight on top of the base value of ε: D = −5 + 5 + 5 = 5, H = −10 + 50 = 40, T = −5, U = 5. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: 50 comes from forgetting D → ε, which contributes −5: taking D = 5 + 5 = 10 gives 10 + 40 + (−5) + 5 = 50. Apply the empty-production value at the end of every chain.
55 results from dropping the ε value of H: H.val = 50 instead of 50 + (−10) gives 5 + 50 − 5 + 5 = 55.
65 results from ignoring all three negative ε values, those of D, H and T (D = 10, H = 50, T = 0, U = 5, so 10 + 50 + 0 + 5).

recognize.clues: A table of productions with semantic rules that add numbers, and a short concrete input string whose value is asked for.
recognize.contrast: An inherited-attribute definition would pass values down from parents or left siblings; here each rule uses only the children's values, so one bottom-up pass is enough.

check.body: Recompute without the grammar: each M adds 5, each L adds 50 and the K adds 5, which is 5 + 5 + 50 + 5 = 65 if nothing else counted. The three empty productions then subtract 5, 10 and 5, a total of 20, giving the same value as the tree evaluation.

code.text:
L1:  t1 = -1
L2:  t2 = 0

L4:  t4 = 4 * t3
L5:  t5 = 4 * t2
L6:  t6 = t5 * M

L8:  t8 = a[t7]
L9:  if t8 <= max goto L11
L10: t1 = t8
L11: t3 = t3 + 1
L12: if t3 < M goto L4
L13: t2 = t2 + 1
L14: if t2 < N goto L3

solutionDiagram.alt: The 15 instructions cut into seven boxes of sizes 2, 1, 6, 1, 2, 2 and 1; the largest is L4 to L9.

steps.title: Basic block and leader
steps.body: A basic block is a maximal run of instructions entered only at its first instruction and left only at its last. Its first instruction is a leader. Leaders are: the first instruction; any instruction that is the target of a jump; any instruction right after a jump.

steps.title: Find the leaders
steps.body: First instruction: L1. Targets: L11 (from L9), L4 (from L12), L3 (from L14). After a jump: L10 (after L9), L13 (after L12), L15 (after L14). Leaders: L1, L3, L4, L10, L11, L13, L15. Seven leaders, so 7 blocks.

steps.title: Sizes and match
steps.body: Blocks: L1 to L2 (2), L3 (1), L4 to L9 (6), L10 (1), L11 to L12 (2), L13 to L14 (2), L15 (1). The largest is L4 to L9 with 6 instructions. So 7 blocks and 6 instructions, option D.

shortcut.body: Mark every jump and its target on the margin. Leaders are the first line, each target, each line after a jump; counting them gives the blocks, and the longest gap between leaders gives the largest block (L4 to L10 gap = 6). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Missing that L3 is a leader (target of the jump at L14) and L10 follows a jump; counting 6 blocks.
6 blocks and size 7 counts L10 into the block L4 to L9, forgetting that L10 starts a new block because L9 is a conditional jump.
7 and 7 has the right count of blocks but sizes the largest one as 7: it counts L10, the leader that starts the next block, as the end of L4 to L9 (an off-by-one at the block boundary).

recognize.clues: A numbered list of three-address instructions with conditional and unconditional jumps, and a question about how many blocks it forms and how large the biggest is.
recognize.contrast: A DAG of a block merges repeated expressions inside one block; here the work comes before that, deciding where the blocks start and end.

check.body: The sizes of all blocks must add up to the number of instructions in the listing, 15. Each leader must also be either line 1, a goto target or the line after a jump, and no jump may appear anywhere except the last line of a block.

questions.stem: Consider the following program. Which one of the following options represents the activation tree corresponding to the main function?
questions.figure: Four activation trees. (A) main has children f1, f2, f3 in that order; f2 has children f3 and f2; the inner f2 has children f3 and f1. (B) main has children f1, f2, f3; f2 has children f3 and f1. (C) main has one child f1; f1 has one child f2; f2 has children f3 and f1. (D) main has children f1, f2, f3; f2 has three children f3, f2, f1.

diagram.alt: Four small trees labelled A to D with main at the root and calls f1, f2, f3 below it; only A nests a second f2 under the first f2.

solutionDiagram.alt: The correct activation tree with each call numbered in order: f1 (1), f2(2) (2), f3 (3), f2(1) (4), f3 (5), f1 (6), f3 (7).

options: main calls f1, f2, f3 in order. f2 calls f3 and f2. The inner f2 calls f3 and f1.
main calls f1, f2, f3 in order. f2 calls f3 and f1.
main calls f1. f1 calls f2. f2 calls f3 and f1.
main calls f1, f2, f3 in order. f2 calls f3, f2 and f1.

steps.title: What an activation tree is
steps.body: Each call to a procedure is an activation. The activation tree has one node per activation. The root is the main call. An activation's children are the calls it makes directly, in the order they start from left to right. A call that is made twice appears twice, and a recursive call appears as a child of the call that makes it.

steps.title: Trace main
steps.body: main makes three calls in order: f1(), f2(2), f3(). f1 calls nothing. f3 calls nothing. Only f2(2) has children.

steps.title: Trace f2(2)
steps.body: f2(2) first calls f3(). X is 2, not 1, so it goes to the else branch and calls f2(1). So f2(2) has two children in order: f3, then f2(1).

steps.title: Trace f2(1)
steps.body: f2(1) calls f3() first. X is 1, so it then calls f1(). It makes no further recursive call. So f2(1) has children f3, then f1. The tree matches option A: the outer f2 has children f3 and f2, and the inner f2 has children f3 and f1.

shortcut.body: f2 is called with X = 2, so it recurses exactly once more: a second f2 must appear under the first. Only A (and D, which puts f2, f3 and f1 flat) has an inner f2; D wrongly gives the outer f2 a call to f1. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Option B treats f2(2) as if it stopped at X == 1, skipping the recursive call f2(1).
Option C makes the calls nest (main to f1 to f2) as if each call came from the previous one. They are siblings: f1 has returned before f2 starts.
Option D gives the outer f2 three children, which would mean f2(2) itself calls f1. That call belongs to the inner f2(1).

recognize.clues: Four trees to choose from, a main function that calls others in sequence, and a function that calls itself with a smaller argument.
recognize.contrast: A call stack at one moment shows only the active calls on a path; the activation tree records every call ever made during the whole run.

check.body: Count calls by running the program in your head. main makes 3 calls, f2(2) makes 2 (f3 and f2(1)) and f2(1) makes 2 (f3 and f1), so the tree has 1 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 8 nodes. The correct tree must have exactly 8 nodes, with f2 appearing twice.

An activation tree has one node for every call made. The children of a node are the calls made directly by that activation, in the order they start.
A call that returns before the next call begins gives a sibling, not a descendant. A function that calls itself adds a new node below the node that made the call, once per level of recursion.
Follow the program text for f2 with the argument it receives, then with the smaller argument it passes on. For each activation list the calls it makes before it returns.

main calls h then g(2). g(2) calls g(1) then h. g(1) calls h.

questions.stem: Consider the control flow graph shown. Which one of the following choices correctly lists the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?
questions.figure: Control flow graph with ENTRY and EXIT. ENTRY goes to B1. B1 contains: i = m - 1; j = n; a = 10. B1 goes to B2. B2 contains: i = i + 1; j = j - 1. B2 goes to B3 and to B4. B3 contains: a = 20, and goes to B4. B4 contains: i = a + 1. B4 goes to EXIT and also back to B2.

diagram.alt: Flow graph: B1 (i = m - 1, j = n, a = 10) to B2 (i = i + 1, j = j - 1); B2 to B3 (a = 20) and to B4 (i = a + 1); B3 to B4; B4 to EXIT and back to B2.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same graph with live-out sets: B1 {a,i,j}, B2 {a,j}, B3 {a,j}, B4 {a,i,j}.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: A variable is live at a point if some path from there reads it before writing it. For each block, use(B) is what B reads before writing, and def(B) is what B writes. Then in(B) = use(B) ∪ (out(B) − def(B)), and out(B) is the union of in(S) over the successors S. Nothing is live at EXIT. Because of the back edge B4 to B2, the sets must be iterated until they stop changing.

steps.title: use and def
steps.body: B1: use {m, n}, def {i, j, a}. B2: use {i, j}, def {i, j}. B3: use { }, def {a}. B4: use {a}, def {i}. The successors: B1 to B2; B2 to B3 and B4; B3 to B4; B4 to B2 (and EXIT).

steps.title: Iterate to the fixed point
steps.body: Start with all sets empty. in(B4) = {a}. in(B3) = out(B3) − {a} ∪ ∅ with out(B3) = in(B4) = {a}, so in(B3) = ∅. out(B2) = in(B3) ∪ in(B4) = {a}, so in(B2) = {i, j} ∪ ({a} − {i, j}) = {a, i, j}. out(B4) = in(B2) = {a, i, j}, so in(B4) = {a} ∪ ({a, i, j} − {i}) = {a, j}. Recompute: out(B3) = in(B4) = {a, j}, in(B3) = {j}; out(B2) = {j} ∪ {a, j} = {a, j}; in(B2) = {i, j} ∪ ({a, j} − {i, j}) = {a, i, j}. Now out(B4) = {a, i, j}, in(B4) = {a, j}; unchanged. out(B1) = in(B2) = {a, i, j}.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Live-out: B1 = {a, i, j}, B2 = {a, j}, B3 = {a, j}, B4 = {a, i, j}. That is option D. Notice i is live out of B4 because the back edge reaches B2, which reads i, and a is live out of B2 because the path B2 to B4 skips the assignment in B3.

shortcut.body: Test the loop. B4 leaves to EXIT or back to B2, and B2 reads i and j, so out(B4) must contain i and j; that kills A, B and C's B4 entry. Only D has {a, i, j} for B4. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Ignoring the back edge and the reads in B2: out(B4) must contain i and j, since B2 reads them, so these sets are far too small.
Computing in-sets of the successor from the use sets only, without the back edge, gives sets like B4: {i}. That is a one-pass answer.
Putting i in out(B2) and out(B3): every path from there reaches B4, which writes i before any read. i is not live out of B2 or B3 (it is live out of B4 only because of the back edge to B2).

recognize.clues: The question asks which variables are live at the exit of each block of a flow graph that has a loop back edge.
recognize.contrast: Available expressions run forward and merge by intersection; liveness runs backward and merges by union, because one path that reads the variable is enough.

check.body: Spot-check one variable by path search. For each block exit, ask whether some path from there reaches a read of the variable with no write on the way. The variable a, for example, is read in B4, and the paths B2 to B4 and B4 to B2 to B4 avoid the write in B3, which can be compared with the sets found.

hints.text: For each block, which variables does it read before it writes them, and which does it write? Which direction does the information travel through the graph?
A variable is live at a point if some path from there reads it before writing it. Liveness is about the future, so it is computed backward.
What is live after a block is the union of what is live at the start of each of its successors. What is live at the start of a block is what it reads, plus what is live after it minus what it writes.

Write the read set and write set of every block. Start from the exit with nothing live and repeat the backward equations in reverse block order until no set changes; the loop edge forces a second round.
Take B4 and B2 first. B4 can go to the exit or back to B2, so ask what B2 reads before writing, and let that flow into the live set after B4.

questions.stem: Consider the syntax directed translation given by the following grammar and semantic rules. Here N, I, F and B are non-terminals. N is the starting non-terminal, and #, 0 and 1 are lexical tokens corresponding to input letters "#", "0" and "1", respectively. X.val denotes the synthesized attribute (a numeric value) associated with a non-terminal X. I1 and F1 denote occurrences of I and F on the right hand side of a production, respectively. For the tokens 0 and 1, 0.val = 0 and 1.val = 1. The value computed by the translation scheme for the input string 10#011 is ________. (Rounded off to three decimal places)

solutionDiagram.alt: Parse tree of 10#011 with val on each node: I is 2 for 10, F is 0.375 for 011 (inner F values 0.75 and 0.5), N is 2.375.

steps.title: Parse the string, then evaluate bottom-up
steps.body: All attributes are synthesized, so a node's val is a function of its children's. Parse 10#011 as N → I # F with I deriving 10 and F deriving 011, then compute vals from the leaves upward. A token gives its own digit.

steps.title: The integer part I
steps.body: I → I1 B is left recursive, so 10 parses as I(I(B(1)) B(0)). The inner I = B = 1. Then I.val = 2 × 1 + 0 = 2. This is binary reading of 10, which is 2.

steps.title: The fraction part F
steps.body: F → B F1 is right recursive: 011 is F(B(0), F(B(1), F(B(1)))). Innermost: F = ½ × 1 = 0.5. Middle: F = ½(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. Outer: F = ½(0 + 0.75) = 0.375. This reads 0.011 in binary, which is 0.25 + 0.125 = 0.375.

shortcut.body: Recognise the scheme as binary-to-decimal with a point: 10.011 in binary = 2 + 0.25 + 0.125 = 2.375. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: 5: reading 011 with the rule for I (doubling), which makes it the integer 3 instead of 0.375, and 2 + 3 = 5.

3.5: dropping the halving in both F rules (F → B as B.val, F → B F1 as ½B.val + F1.val) gives 1, 1.5, 1.5, so F = 1.5 and 2 + 1.5 = 3.5. The ½ multiplies the whole sum B.val + F1.val, and F → B halves its leaf.
4: dropping both halves, so F = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 and 2 + 2 = 4.

recognize.clues: Numeric semantic rules attached to productions, a concrete input string with a separator token, and a rounded numeric answer.
recognize.contrast: The left-recursive I rule and the right-recursive F rule look alike, but the first builds a whole number from left to right and the second builds a fraction from the right.

check.body: Treat the input as a binary number with a point. Convert the digits before the point and the digits after it independently, by place value, and add. This route does not use the grammar rules, so it independently confirms the tree evaluation.

The values are synthesized: each node's value is computed from its children, so evaluate from the leaves up to the root.
The I rules double the value so far and add the new digit, which reads digits as a whole number. The F rules halve a combination of the digit and the rest, which reads digits as a fraction.
Split the input at the # token. Evaluate the left part with the I rules from its first digit onward, and the right part with the F rules starting from its last digit, then add the two.
For the right-hand part, start with its last digit alone using the single-digit rule, then work leftward one digit at a time.

questions.stem:
Consider the following grammar along with translation rules.

Here # and % are operators and id is a token that represents an integer and $id.val$ represents the corresponding integer value. The set of non-terminals is $\{S, T, R, P\}$ and a subscripted non-terminal indicates an instance of the non-terminal.

Using this translation scheme, the computed value of $S.val$ for root of the parse tree for the expression 20#10%5#8%2%2 is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Parse tree of 20#10%5#8%2%2: the root S has val 80 from S 40 times T 2; S 40 is S 20 times T 2; the right T is T 4 divided by R 2, and T 4 is T 8 divided by R 2.

steps.title: What the rules mean and what decides the grouping
steps.body: A translation scheme attaches a small formula to each production. A parse tree is the tree of productions that derives the input string, and every node gets an attribute val computed by the formula of the production used at that node. Here val is built only from the children, so it is computed bottom-up: leaves first, root last. Two facts decide everything. First, both recursive rules are left-recursive: S → S1 # T and T → T1 % R put the recursive symbol on the left. A left-recursive rule makes the left operand the larger, already-built subtree, so a chain of the same operator groups from the left. Second, T sits below S in the grammar, so every % chain is finished into one T before any # can use it: % binds tighter than #. In the formulas, # multiplies and % divides.

steps.title: Cut the string at the # symbols
steps.body: The expression 20#10%5#8%2%2 has two # symbols, so the top of the tree applies S → S1 # T twice. Reading left to right, the string splits into three chunks: 20, then 10%5, then 8%2%2. The first chunk is reached by S → T and T → R → id. The other two chunks are the T operands of the two # nodes. The tree in the picture shows exactly this shape.

steps.title: Evaluate each % chunk
steps.body: The chunk 20 is a single id, so its val is 20. The chunk 10%5 uses T → T1 % R once: T.val = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. The chunk 8%2%2 has two % symbols and groups to the left, because T1 is the left recursive instance: the inner T is 8%2 with val 8 ÷ 2 = 4, and the outer T is that T % 2 with val 4 ÷ 2 = 2.

steps.title: Combine with the # rule
steps.body: The leftmost S has S → T, so its val is 20. The next S has S1.val = 20 and T.val = 2, so val = 20 * 2 = 40. The root has S1.val = 40 and T.val = 2, so S.val = 40 * 2 = 80. The answer is 80.

shortcut.body: Split at # first, then do each % chain strictly left to right: 20, 10÷5 = 2, 8÷2÷2 = 2, and multiply: 20 × 2 × 2 = 80. Do not rearrange the % chain; the grammar fixes left grouping, and 8÷(2÷2) would give a different number. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: 320: grouping the % chain to the right, 8 ÷ (2 ÷ 2) = 8, gives 20 * 2 * 8. The rule T → T1 % R is left-recursive, so the chain groups to the left.
0: reading % as the remainder operator, 10 mod 5 = 0 and 8 mod 2 mod 2 = 0, so the product collapses. The translation rule says ÷, not remainder.
160: stopping the second chain at 8%2 = 4 and forgetting the last % 2, which gives 20 * 2 * 4.

recognize.clues: A grammar with two operator levels and left-recursive rules, translation rules that compute from the children, and a concrete expression to evaluate.
recognize.contrast: This is not ordinary arithmetic precedence read from symbols; the grammar fixes the grouping, and the translation rules, not the symbols, give the meaning.

check.body: Evaluate the pieces a second way, as a fraction: the divided chains are 10/5 and 8/2/2, so the whole product is 20 times 10/5 times 8/(2*2). Both routes must produce the same value, and the second does not depend on the order of the steps.

questions.stem: In the context of compilers, which of the following is/are NOT an intermediate representation of the source program?

steps.title: What an intermediate representation is
steps.body: A compiler does not go from source text straight to machine code. In between it builds one or more intermediate representations (IR): forms of the program itself, with its operations and their order, that the later phases can analyse and rewrite. The test for any candidate is whether you could read the program back out of it. A symbol table is different in kind. It is a lookup table that maps each name to facts such as its type, scope and storage address. Every phase reads and writes it, but it holds no statements.

steps.title: Test the four candidates
steps.body: Three address code is a linear IR: a list of instructions with at most three addresses each, such as t1 = b + c. An abstract syntax tree is a tree IR built by the parser: each operator is a node and its operands are the children. A control flow graph is a graph IR whose nodes are basic blocks of three address code and whose edges are possible jumps; optimizers work on it. All three describe the program, so they are IRs. The symbol table describes names only, so it is not.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only the symbol table is NOT an intermediate representation, which is option D.

shortcut.body: Ask of each option: does it contain the program's operations? Code lists, trees and flow graphs do; a table of names does not. Pick the one that is a dictionary. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing the AST because it comes straight from the parser and feels like part of parsing rather than an IR. A syntax tree is the usual high-level IR, so it is an IR.
Choosing the CFG because a graph is not code. The CFG is the structure that data-flow analyses such as liveness run on, and it is a standard IR.
Adding the symbol table to the set of IRs because it is built early and used by all phases is the reverse mistake, and the question is an MSQ: all of A, B and C must be left unmarked.

recognize.clues: The wording asks which items are NOT an intermediate representation, and the options mix program forms with a data structure.
recognize.contrast: A symbol table is used by every phase like an IR is, but it records names and their attributes, not the program's operations.

check.body: For each option, try to describe how one assignment such as a = b + c is stored in it. If a clear entry for that operation exists, it is an IR; if the only thing stored is a name with its type or address, it is not.

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI C code segment, given below the question.

Assume that the variable y points to a struct (allocated on the heap) containing two fields f1 and f2, and the local variables x, y, z, p, q, and i are allotted registers. Common sub-expression elimination (CSE) optimization is applied on the code. The number of addition and dereference operations (of the form y->f1 or y->f2) in the optimized code, respectively, are:

steps.title: What CSE does and what we count
steps.body: Common sub-expression elimination finds an expression that is computed more than once with the same operand values, computes it a single time into a temporary, and reuses the temporary. It is legal only while no operand changes between the uses. We count run-time operations of the optimized code: each executed + is one addition, and each executed y->f1 or y->f2 is one dereference (a load from the heap). Register accesses are free.

steps.title: Find the repeated expressions
steps.body: x + 3 appears in the first line, in the if branch (p = p + x + 3) and in the else branch (q = q + x + 3). y->f1 appears in the first line and in the if branch. y->f2 appears in the first line and in the else branch. Nothing in the fragment assigns to x, to y, or to a field of y, so all three values stay the same for the whole run and can be computed once, before the loop: t1 = x + 3, t2 = y->f1, t3 = y->f2.

steps.title: Cost before the loop
steps.body: z = t1 + t2 + t3 needs the addition that builds t1 plus two more, so 3 additions. The two dereferences are y->f1 and y->f2, so 2 dereferences.

steps.title: Cost of one loop iteration
steps.body: The values of i are 0, 2, 4, ..., 198, which is 100 iterations. Each iteration executes i = i + 2, one addition. The if branch executes p = p + t1 and q = q + t2, two additions; the else branch executes p = p + t3 and q = q + t1, also two additions. Neither branch dereferences anything now. So every iteration costs 1 + 2 = 3 additions and 0 dereferences, whichever branch runs.

steps.title: Total and option
steps.body: Additions: 3 + 300 = 303. Dereferences: 2. That is option D.

shortcut.body: Dereferences first: y->f1 and y->f2 are never written, so CSE keeps them in registers and only 2 remain. That removes A and C. For additions, count per iteration: the loop step plus the two accumulations is 3, so 3 * 100 = 300, plus 3 before the loop: 303. Option B (203) forgets the loop increment. About 2 minutes. The load reuse is safe only because nothing in the fragment may write through a pointer into the struct.

traps.text: 403 and 102 is the code with no CSE at all: 3 + 100 * 4 additions (x + 3 recomputed inside each branch) and 2 + 100 dereferences. The question asks for the optimized code.
203 and 2 gets the dereferences right but forgets that i = i + 2 is an addition executed 100 times, so it counts only 3 + 100 * 2.
303 and 102 removes the repeated x + 3 but keeps reloading y->f1 and y->f2 in the loop. These loads are also common sub-expressions: nothing changes the fields, so they can live in registers.

recognize.clues: The question names common sub-expression elimination and asks for operation counts in the optimized code, with x + 3, y->f1 and y->f2 each written more than once.
recognize.contrast: Plain dead-code or constant folding removes work that is useless or known at compile time; here the work is useful but repeated, so the fix is to compute it once and reuse it.

check.body: Count the code without CSE and subtract what CSE saves. Unoptimized, the first line costs 3 additions and 2 dereferences, and each pass costs 1 for the loop step plus 3 and 1 dereference in either branch, so 3 + 100 * 4 = 403 additions and 2 + 100 = 102 dereferences. CSE removes the repeated x + 3 and one load per pass, 100 additions and 100 dereferences, which leaves the value found in the steps.

questions.stem:
For a statement $S$ in a program, in the context of liveness analysis, the following sets are defined:

$USE(S)$: the set of variables used in $S$
$IN(S)$: the set of variables that are live at the entry of $S$
$OUT(S)$: the set of variables that are live at the exit of $S$

Consider a basic block that consists of two statements, $S_1$ followed by $S_2$. Which one of the following statements is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: S1 and S2 as two boxes in a row with arrows through them; the arrow between them is labelled OUT of S1 equals IN of S2.

steps.title: Live variables and the two flow equations
steps.body: A variable is live at a point if some path from that point reads it before writing it. IN(S) is the live set just before statement S runs and OUT(S) is the live set just after. Liveness runs backward. Two equations define it. First, what is live after S is whatever any successor needs: OUT(S) is the union of IN(T) over every successor T of S. Second, what is live before S is what S reads, plus what is live after S and not overwritten by S: IN(S) = USE(S) ∪ (OUT(S) − DEF(S)), where DEF(S) is the set of variables S writes.
steps.tex: OUT(S) = \bigcup_{T \in succ(S)} IN(T), \qquad IN(S) = USE(S) \cup \big(OUT(S) - DEF(S)\big)

steps.title: Apply the first equation to S1
steps.body: Inside a basic block control flows straight from S1 to S2, so S2 is the only successor of S1. The union has a single term, and OUT(S1) = IN(S2) with nothing added and nothing removed. This is option A.

steps.title: Why the other options fail
steps.body: Take S1: a = b and S2: c = a, with c live after the block. Then IN(S2) = {a}, so OUT(S1) = {a}, and IN(S1) = {b}. Option B gives IN(S1) ∪ USE(S1) = {b}. Option C gives IN(S2) ∪ OUT(S2) = {a, c}. Option D gives USE(S1) ∪ IN(S2) = {a, b}. Only option A gives {a}.

shortcut.body: Liveness at the exit of a statement is liveness at the entry of whatever runs next. For one straight-line successor that is a plain equality, so only A can be right. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: This runs the IN equation backward. IN(S1) is computed from OUT(S1), not the other way round, and the right side {b} in the example is not what S2 needs.

Adding OUT(S2) puts back variables that S2 itself writes. In the example c is live after S2 but S2 overwrites it, so c is not live between S1 and S2. IN(S2) already contains the part of OUT(S2) that survives S2.
Adding USE(S1) mixes up the statement's own reads with its live-out set. What S1 reads is needed before S1, so it belongs in IN(S1), not in OUT(S1).

recognize.clues: The wording defines USE, IN and OUT for statements in a basic block and asks which relation between consecutive statements is correct, which is the backward liveness equation.
recognize.contrast: Reaching definitions run forward and join over predecessors; liveness runs backward and joins over successors, so the dependency goes from the later statement to the earlier one.

check.body: Use three statements: S1: t = u + v, S2: u = t, S3: w = u + v, with only w live at the exit. Going backward, IN(S3) = {u, v}, so OUT(S2) = {u, v}, then IN(S2) = {t} union ({u, v} minus {u}) = {t, v}. The set between S1 and S2 must therefore be {t, v}. Option B gives {u, v}, option C gives {t, u, v}, option D gives {t, u, v}, and only option A gives {t, v}.

hints.text: In which direction does information about future reads travel through a block, and what does the statement after S1 need from the state before it?
A variable is live at a point if some path from that point reads it before writing it. IN is the live set before a statement and OUT is the live set after it.
The live set after a statement is built only from the statements that can run next. A statement does not feed its own reads into the set that follows it.
Pick a tiny example with two assignments and a known set live at the end of the block. Compute IN of the second statement, then ask which options reproduce that set for the point between the two.

variation.stem: A basic block has S1: x = y + z followed by S2: w = x + y. The variables live at the exit of the block are w and z. Which set is OUT(S1), the set live between the two statements?
variation.explanation: OUT(S1) equals IN(S2), since S2 is the only successor of S1. IN(S2) = USE(S2) union (OUT(S2) minus DEF(S2)) = {x, y} union ({w, z} minus {w}) = $\{x, y, z\}$. The set $\{y, z\}$ is IN(S1), which is the point before S1, not between the statements.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.

$S_1$: The sequence of procedure calls corresponds to a preorder traversal of the activation tree.
$S_2$: The sequence of procedure returns corresponds to a postorder traversal of the activation tree.

Which one of the following options is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Activation tree with main calling f then g, and f calling h then k. Each node is labelled with the order of its call and the order of its return: calls main, f, h, k, g; returns h, k, f, g, main.

steps.title: Activations and the activation tree
steps.body: One execution of a procedure body is an activation. The activation tree has a node for every activation. The root is the activation of main, and the children of a node are the activations that node starts directly, ordered left to right by the time they were called. Two traversals matter. Preorder visits a node first and then its children from left to right. Postorder visits the children from left to right and then the node. The fact that decides the question is that procedure calls nest: a callee always finishes before its caller continues.

steps.title: Calls give preorder
steps.body: A node is created at the moment its procedure is called. After that, the procedure starts its children one by one, left to right, and each child's whole subtree is called before the next child. So the call order is node, then first child's subtree, then the second child's subtree: preorder. Statement S1 is true.

steps.title: Returns give postorder
steps.body: A procedure returns only after every activation it started has returned, and those return in the order they were called. So the return order is the first child's subtree, the second child's subtree, and then the node itself: postorder. Statement S2 is true. In the picture, main calls f and g, and f calls h and k. Calls happen as main, f, h, k, g, and returns as h, k, f, g, main. Both statements hold, which is option C.

shortcut.body: Calls are entering a node and returns are leaving it, exactly like a depth-first walk. Enter order is preorder and leave order is postorder, so both are true. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Thinking returns are the exact reverse of calls because the call stack is last in, first out. Reverse call order is g, k, h, f, main in the example, but the real return order is h, k, f, g, main. The stack discipline applies to the activations alive at one moment, not to the whole sequence.
Reading calls as level order because main starts f and g 'first'. g is not called until f and all of f's descendants have finished, so the order is depth first.
Rejecting both because the activation tree is 'not an ordinary tree'. It is an ordinary ordered tree, and calls and returns are its depth-first entry and exit.

recognize.clues: The statements talk about the sequence of procedure calls and returns and the shape of the activation tree, which is the run-time view of nested calls.
recognize.contrast: The control stack holds only the activations alive at one moment and pops in reverse order of pushing; the activation tree records every activation ever made, so the full sequence of returns is not the reverse of the calls.

check.body: Use a deeper tree: main calls a and then d, and a calls b, which calls c. Calls occur as main, a, b, c, d and returns as c, b, a, d, main. Walk the tree depth first: listing a node on entry gives the call list, listing it on exit gives the return list, so both statements hold even when a callee has its own callee.

hints.text: At the moment a procedure is called, which activations already exist, and in what order can its callees start and finish?
An activation tree has a node for every execution of a procedure body. The children of a node are the calls it makes directly, ordered left to right by time.
Calls nest: a callee must finish before its caller continues. Compare that with the two depth-first orders, one that lists a node on entry and one that lists it on exit.
Draw a small tree with a root that calls two procedures, one of which calls another. Write the order of calls and the order of returns beside it, then test each statement against both lists.

variation.stem: In a run, main calls p and then q. The procedure p calls r, and the procedure q calls s and then t. Which option lists the order in which these procedures return?
options: t, s, q, r, p, main
r, p, s, t, q, main
r, s, t, p, q, main
main, p, r, q, s, t
variation.explanation: Returns follow the postorder of the activation tree. The leaf r returns before p, then the subtree of q returns as s, t and then q, and main returns last, giving r, p, s, t, q, main. Reversing the call order main, p, r, q, s, t would treat the whole run as one stack, which is wrong.

questions.stem:
Consider the following grammar (that admits a series of declarations, followed by expressions) and the associated syntax directed translation (SDT) actions, given as pseudo-code (see the table below).

With respect to the above grammar, which one of the following choices is correct?

rows: {record that ID.lexeme is of type int}
{record that ID.lexeme is of type bool}
{check that E1.type = E2.type = int; set E.type := int}
{check that E1.type = bool; set E.type := bool}

options: The actions can be used to correctly type-check any syntactically correct program.
The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct integer variable declarations and integer expressions.
The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct boolean variable declarations and boolean expressions.
The actions will lead to an infinite loop.

steps.title: What these actions do
steps.body: A syntax directed translation attaches an action to each production, and the action runs when the parser reduces by that production. Type checking means an action compares the types of the operands and either accepts or reports an error, and sets the type of the new node for the actions above it. The decisive question for any such scheme is where the types come from at the bottom of the expression: a check can only be as good as the type that the leaf rule hands up. Here the leaf rule is E → ID.

steps.title: The leaf rule hands up int every time
steps.body: The action for E → ID sets E.type := int. It never looks up what the declarations recorded for that identifier. So every identifier in an expression is treated as an int, whether it was declared int or bool. The declaration actions record types but nothing reads them.

steps.title: Integer part works
steps.body: For int declarations and integer expressions the leaf type int is correct, and the E1 + E2 check (both operands int) and its result type int are correct. So the actions can type-check integer declarations and integer expressions: statement B is true.

steps.title: Boolean part and the rest fail
steps.body: For a boolean expression the rule E → !E1 needs E1.type = bool. The only way to get a bool is another !E, and the innermost operand of any ! chain is an ID or a sum, both of type int, so the check always fails. A bool variable used in an expression is wrongly seen as int. So C is false, and A is false for the same reason. The actions have no recursion that could loop: each one runs once per node of a finite parse tree, so D is false. The answer is B.

shortcut.body: Look at the base case of the expressions: E → ID always gives int. Anything that needs bool as its operand can never be satisfied, which removes A and C. An action does not loop, which removes D. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: 'Any syntactically correct program' over-claims. A program with a bool declaration and a ! applied to that variable is syntactically correct but is rejected by these actions, because the variable is typed int.

Pairing the bool declaration action with the ! action looks like a full boolean checker. The missing piece is that E → ID does not read the recorded declaration, so no expression can ever have type bool.
The star in D* E* only describes repetition in the grammar. The actions run once per parse tree node and never call themselves, so nothing can loop.

recognize.clues: A grammar with declarations followed by expressions, actions that set E.type and check operand types, and a question about what the actions can type-check.
recognize.contrast: This is attribute evaluation on a finished parse tree, not a parsing question: the grammar itself accepts every program, and the actions decide which of them are well typed.

check.body: Test the claim with two tiny programs: one that declares an integer and adds it to itself, and one that declares a boolean and negates it. Run the leaf rule and the operator rules for each, and see which program the actions accept and which they wrongly reject.
