hints.text: Where does the type of an identifier inside an expression come from in these actions, and what do the declaration actions do with the types they record?
A syntax directed translation attaches an action to each production and runs it when the parser reduces by that production. The action computes the type of the new node from its children.
Look at the production for an identifier inside an expression. Ask whether its action consults anything the declarations stored, or fixes the type by itself.
Take a short program that declares one variable of each type and uses each in an expression. Evaluate the leaf rule and the operator rules for it, and see which option still holds.

variation.stem: Variables a (int) and b (bool) are declared. The actions are: E -> ID takes the type recorded for the identifier; E -> E1 + E2 requires both operands int and gives int; E -> !E1 requires bool and gives bool. How many of the expressions a + a, !b, a + !b and !!b pass the type check?
variation.explanation: With the leaf type read from the declaration, a + a passes, !b passes, !!b passes, and a + !b fails because the right operand of + is bool. That is 3 expressions. Giving every identifier type int would accept only a + a, which is 1.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C code segment (given below the question).

In a compiler, this code segment is represented internally as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The number of nodes in the DAG is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: DAG with leaves b, c and 1. One plus node over b and c is labelled a, d. One plus node over that node and 1 is labelled e, f. The top plus node is labelled g and has two edges to the e, f node. Six nodes in all.

steps.title: The DAG of a basic block
steps.body: A DAG for straight-line code has one node for each distinct value. A leaf stands for a value that exists when the block starts: a variable or a constant. An interior node stands for an operator applied to two earlier nodes. Each variable name is attached as a label to the node holding its current value. The rule that makes it a DAG and not a tree is reuse: when a statement applies the same operator to the same two nodes as an existing node, it does not make a new node; it attaches the new name to the old one. This is common sub-expression elimination drawn as a graph.

steps.title: Build it statement by statement
steps.body: a = b + c: make leaves b and c and an interior node n1 = (b + c). Label n1 with a. e = a + 1: a is n1; make a leaf for the constant 1 and a node n2 = (n1 + 1). Label n2 with e. d = b + c: the same operator on the same nodes as n1, so reuse n1 and add the label d. f = d + 1: d is n1, so this is n1 + 1, which is n2; add the label f. g = e + f: both e and f are n2, so make one new node n3 = (n2 + n2), with two edges to n2. Label n3 with g.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Leaves: b, c and 1, which is 3. Interior nodes: n1, n2, n3, which is 3. The total is 6.

shortcut.body: Count leaves (b, c, 1) and then count distinct operator applications: b+c, (b+c)+1 and the sum of the last two. d and f repeat earlier ones, so they add nothing. 3 + 3 = 6. About 1 minute. This works because b and c are not reassigned inside the block.

traps.text: 8: giving every statement its own node (5 interior nodes) and adding the 3 leaves. That ignores that d = b + c and f = d + 1 repeat earlier computations.
5: counting the five assigned variables, or five interior nodes with no sharing, and leaving out the leaves b, c and the constant 1, which are nodes of the DAG too.

recognize.clues: Straight-line assignments with repeated sub-expressions and a request for the number of nodes of the DAG representation of the block.
recognize.contrast: A syntax tree would give every occurrence its own node; a DAG merges equal sub-expressions, so the node count is the number of distinct values, which is smaller.

check.body: Count a second way. List the distinct operator applications over distinct operand nodes, then add the distinct leaves that the statements read before writing. The total from this list must match the node count from the step-by-step build, and every assigned name should appear as a label on exactly one node.

hints.text: Which of the five statements compute a value that an earlier statement already produced, and what are the starting values that no statement computes?
A DAG for a basic block has one node per distinct value: a leaf for each variable or constant that exists at entry and an interior node for each operator applied to two nodes.
When a statement applies the same operator to the same two nodes as an existing node, no new node is made; the new name is only attached as a label of the old one.
Go statement by statement, keeping a table from each name to its current node. Look up the operands in the table, then check whether the same operator over the same nodes already exists.
The first statement makes two leaves and one operator node. Check whether the third statement needs a new node or reuses that one, before moving on.

variation.stem: A basic block is represented as a DAG: p = m + n; q = p * 2; r = m + n; s = r * 2; t = q - s; u = t + p. The variables m and n are not assigned in the block. How many nodes does the DAG have?
variation.explanation: The leaves are m, n and the constant 2. The interior nodes are m + n (labelled p and r), the product with 2 (labelled q and s), q - s over those two shared nodes (labelled t), and t + p (labelled u). That is 3 leaves plus 4 interior nodes, 7 in all.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.

I. Symbol table is accessed only during lexical analysis and syntax analysis.
II. Compilers for programming languages that support recursion necessarily need heap storage for memory allocation in the run-time environment.
III. Errors violating the condition 'any variable must be declared before its use' are detected during syntax analysis.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
options: None of I, II, and III

steps.title: The terms and the test
steps.body: A compiler works in phases. Lexical analysis cuts the text into tokens. Syntax analysis checks that the tokens fit the grammar and builds the parse tree. Semantic analysis checks meaning, such as types and declarations. Later phases make intermediate code, optimize and generate machine code. The symbol table is the shared dictionary of names with their type, scope and address. At run time the program has three kinds of storage: static data, the stack of activation records (one per active procedure call), and the heap for memory requested explicitly with malloc or new. The test for each statement is: which phase or which storage does the claim really involve?

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: The symbol table is not limited to the first two phases. Semantic analysis looks names up to check types and declarations, and code generation reads the addresses stored there. 'Only during lexical and syntax analysis' is false.

steps.title: Statement II
steps.body: Recursion needs many live copies of a procedure's locals at the same time. The stack of activation records supplies exactly that, one record per call, freed when the call returns. The heap is for data that outlives a call, and a recursive function that allocates nothing never touches it. 'Necessarily need heap storage' is false.

steps.title: Statement III and the answer
steps.body: Syntax is described by a context-free grammar, which cannot remember which names were declared earlier. 'Declared before use' is a context-sensitive condition. It is checked in semantic analysis by looking the name up in the symbol table. So III is false, and no statement is true: option D.

shortcut.body: Each statement carries an absolute word: 'only', 'necessarily', and a phase claim. Test each against one fact: the symbol table is used by every later phase, recursion uses the stack, and declaration checks are semantic. All three fail. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Believing the symbol table is finished once parsing ends. Type checking and code generation both consult it, so I is false.
Calling an undeclared variable a syntax error because the compiler reports it near the parser's line number. The grammar cannot express the rule, so the check belongs to semantic analysis.
Linking recursion with the heap, since recursion 'grows memory'. The growth is the stack of activation records, not heap allocation.

recognize.clues: Three statements that each tie a compiler phase or storage area to a task, with absolute words such as only and necessarily.
recognize.contrast: Syntax analysis checks the shape of the token sequence with a context-free grammar; checks that depend on earlier declarations belong to semantic analysis, which is a separate phase.

check.body: Look for a counterexample to each statement. For the symbol table, name a later phase that reads it. For recursion, picture a recursive function that allocates nothing on the heap. For declaration checks, ask whether a context-free grammar can remember earlier names.

hints.text: For each statement, which phase of the compiler or which kind of run-time storage does the claim really involve?
The symbol table is a shared dictionary of names. Run-time storage has static data, a stack of activation records and a heap for explicit requests.
Words like only and necessarily make a claim false the moment one counterexample exists. Find a phase, or a program, that breaks each statement.
List the phases in order and mark which of them read the symbol table. For recursion, ask what must exist per call, and whether any explicit allocation request is needed for that.

variation.stem:
Consider the statements.
I. The parse tree is built during lexical analysis.
II. Checking that a call passes as many arguments as the procedure declares is done in semantic analysis.
III. A language that supports recursion needs one activation record for each active call.
Which of the above are TRUE?
variation.explanation: Lexical analysis produces tokens, and the parse tree is built in syntax analysis, so I is false. Argument counts depend on declarations, which a context-free grammar cannot track, so the check is semantic and II is true. Recursion keeps several calls of one procedure alive at once, so each needs its own record, and III is true.

questions.stem:
Consider the productions A → PQ and A → XY. Each of the five non-terminals A, P, Q, X, and Y has two attributes: $s$ is a synthesized attribute, and $i$ is an inherited attribute. Consider the following rules (Rule 1 belongs to A → PQ and Rule 2 to A → XY).

Rule 1: $P.i = A.i + 2$, $Q.i = P.i + A.i$, and $A.s = P.s + Q.s$

Rule 2: $X.i = A.i + Y.s$ and $Y.i = X.s + A.i$

Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Both Rule 1 and Rule 2 are L-attributed.
Neither Rule 1 nor Rule 2 is L-attributed.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two dependency diagrams. For Rule 1 every arrow comes from the parent A or from the left sibling P. For Rule 2 a red arrow goes from Y.s to X.i, from the right sibling to the left one.

steps.title: The vocabulary and the L-attributed test
steps.body: A synthesized attribute of a node is computed from the attributes of its children, so information flows up. An inherited attribute of a node is computed from its parent and its siblings, so information flows down or sideways. A definition is L-attributed when every inherited attribute of a symbol on the right side of a production uses only: the inherited attributes of the left-side symbol (the parent), and any attributes of symbols to its left in the same production. The letter L stands for left: then one left-to-right depth-first walk of the tree can compute everything. A synthesized attribute of the left-side symbol may use anything on the right, with no restriction.

steps.title: Check Rule 1, production A → PQ
steps.body: P.i = A.i + 2 uses the parent's inherited attribute, which is allowed. Q.i = P.i + A.i uses P, which is to the left of Q, and the parent's A.i, so it is allowed. A.s = P.s + Q.s is a synthesized attribute of the parent, so it is unrestricted. Every inherited attribute passes, so Rule 1 is L-attributed.

steps.title: Check Rule 2, production A → XY
steps.body: X.i = A.i + Y.s depends on Y.s, and Y is to the right of X. Even though s is synthesized, the position decides: X would need a value from a symbol that a left-to-right walk has not reached yet. Rule 2 breaks the test. (Y.i = X.s + A.i is fine on its own.) Only Rule 1 is L-attributed: option B.

shortcut.body: Underline every inherited attribute (the .i on the left of each equation) and look at its right side for a symbol that stands to its right in the production. X.i = A.i + Y.s has Y to the right, so Rule 2 fails; nothing similar occurs in Rule 1. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Treating Y.s as harmless because s is synthesized. Whether an attribute is synthesized does not matter for the test; what matters is that Y sits to the right of X, so the value is not available in a left-to-right pass.
Reversing the two rules. The sideways dependency in Rule 1, Q.i from P.i, goes from left to right and is legal; the one in Rule 2 goes from right to left.
Rejecting Rule 1 because Q.i uses both a sibling's attribute and the parent's. The test allows both, as long as the sibling is on the left.

recognize.clues: Two sets of attribute equations over two productions, mixing inherited and synthesized attributes, with the question of whether they are L-attributed.
recognize.contrast: S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and suit bottom-up evaluation; L-attributed ones may also use inherited attributes, but only from the parent and from left siblings.

check.body: Try to evaluate each rule in one left-to-right walk of the children. At each child, list the values it needs and mark whether they already exist when the walk arrives. A rule that needs a value from a symbol visited later cannot be evaluated this way.

hints.text: For each inherited attribute in a rule, which symbols does its right side read, and where do those symbols stand in the production?
An inherited attribute takes its value from the parent or from siblings. A synthesized attribute takes its value from the children.

A definition is L-attributed when each inherited attribute of a right-side symbol reads only the parent inherited attributes and attributes of symbols to its left. The parent synthesized attribute is not restricted.
For each rule, underline the inherited attributes on the left of the equals sign. Write the position of each symbol on the right side and compare it with the position of the symbol being defined.

variation.stem: Consider the productions A -> PQ and A -> XY. Rule 1 (for A -> PQ): P.i = Q.s + 1, Q.i = A.i, A.s = P.s + Q.s. Rule 2 (for A -> XY): X.i = 2 * A.i, Y.i = X.s + A.i, A.s = Y.s. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Both Rule 1 and Rule 2 are L-attributed.
Neither Rule 1 nor Rule 2 is L-attributed.
variation.explanation: In Rule 1, P.i reads Q.s, and Q stands to the right of P, so it cannot be known when the left-to-right walk reaches P. Rule 1 is not L-attributed. In Rule 2, X.i reads only the parent, Y.i reads the left sibling X and the parent, and A.s is a parent synthesized attribute, so Rule 2 is L-attributed.

questions.stem:
Consider the following grammar and the semantic actions to support the inherited type declaration attributes. Let $X_1$, $X_2$, $X_3$, $X_4$, $X_5$, and $X_6$ be the placeholders for the non-terminals D, T, L or $L_1$ in the following table:

Which one of the following are the appropriate choices for $X_1$, $X_2$, $X_3$ and $X_4$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Parse tree of the declaration int a, b with D over T and L. A red arrow carries the type from T to L, and a second red arrow carries it from L down to L1, which owns id a.

steps.title: What is being passed and which way
steps.body: In a declaration such as int a, b, the type is written once, at the front, but every name in the list needs it. In the grammar, T builds the type: T → int sets T.type = int, which is a synthesized attribute computed from the child. The names are created by L, deeper in the tree and to the right of T. So the type must travel to L, and from L down to each smaller list L1, until addType(id.entry, ...) stores it for an id. An attribute that receives its value from the parent or from a left sibling is an inherited attribute, so the type in L is inherited. In a rule X.type = Y.type, the left side X receives and the right side Y gives.

steps.title: Fill the rule for D → T L
steps.body: The type is known at T and needed at L, which is T's right sibling. So L receives it from T: L.type = T.type. Hence X1 = L and X2 = T.

steps.title: Fill the rule for L → L1 , id
steps.body: The list L has the type, and its inner list L1 needs it for the identifiers before the comma. So L1 receives it from its parent: L1.type = L.type. Hence X3 = L1 and X4 = L. The addType call then stores the type for id using L's value, so X5 = L, and X6 = L in the rule L → id.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: X1 = L, X2 = T, X3 = L1, X4 = L is option A.

shortcut.body: Think of a copy that moves from the declared type towards the names. The receiver is on the left of '=': it must be L in the first rule (T is the source) and L1 in the second (L is the source). Only option A has this shape. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Writing T.type = L.type reverses the flow. T.type is already fixed by T → int or T → float, and L has nothing to give yet. The second rule X3 = L1, X4 = T also names T, which is not part of the production L → L1 , id.
X1 = L and X2 = L makes the first rule L.type = L.type, which copies a value to itself and never brings the type in. X4 = T has the same problem: T is not a symbol of L → L1 , id.
Both rules run the wrong way: T.type = L.type has T receiving, and T.type = L1.type uses a T that does not appear in the production for L.

recognize.clues: A declaration grammar where the type is given once by T and every identifier in the list L needs it, with the placeholders standing for the receiving and giving symbols of each copy rule.
recognize.contrast: A synthesized copy would carry the type up from the identifiers to T; here the type is carried down and sideways, which is the inherited direction.

check.body: Run the chosen assignments on the declaration int a, b. Start at T with int, pass it to L by the first rule, then to L1 by the second rule, and store it at each identifier. If every identifier receives int and no rule uses a symbol outside its production, the choice is consistent.

hints.text: The type is written once at the front of a declaration, but several names need it. Which symbol knows the type, and which symbols need to receive it?
An inherited attribute receives its value from the parent or a left sibling. In a rule X.type = Y.type, the left side receives and the right side gives.
The value must travel from where it is computed to where it is used. Check that each symbol named in a rule is actually part of that rule's production.
For D -> T L, decide which of T and L already has a type and which needs one. Repeat for L -> L1 , id with the symbols L and L1, then look for the option that matches both.

$X_1 = Names,\ X_2 = Kind,\ X_3 = Names_1,\ X_4 = Names$

questions.stem:
Consider the following intermediate program in three address code (shown below the question).

Which one of the following corresponds to a static single assignment form of the above code?

code.text:
p = a - b
q = p * c
p = u * v
q = p + q

steps.title: Static single assignment form
steps.body: A program is in static single assignment (SSA) form when every variable name is assigned in exactly one place in the program text. To get there, each assignment to p or q is given a new numbered name (p1, p2, ...), and every use is rewritten to the name of the definition that reaches it. In straight-line code the reaching definition of a use is the last assignment before it. Two conditions decide whether a rewrite is SSA of the given code: no name appears on the left of two statements, and every right-hand name is the one the original program would have read. The numbers themselves are only labels; they need not start at 1 or be consecutive.

steps.title: Which definitions the original uses read
steps.body: Line 2 reads p from line 1. Line 4 reads p from line 3 (the second assignment to p) and q from line 2 (not from line 4 itself, which only defines q after it reads). So in the answer, line 2 must read the name defined on line 1, and line 4 must read the names defined on lines 3 and 2.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Option A defines p1 twice and q1 twice, so it is not single assignment. Option C is single assignment on the left, but line 2 reads p2, and line 4 reads p4 and q3, names that no statement defines. Option D leaves p and q unnumbered on the right, so the reader cannot tell which of the several definitions of p is meant. Option B defines p3, q4, p4, q5, all different; line 2 reads p3 (line 1), line 4 reads p4 (line 3) and q4 (line 2). It satisfies both conditions.

shortcut.body: First scan the left-hand sides for a repeated name: A fails. Then check that every right-hand name appears on some left-hand side above it: C and D fail. Only B survives. About 45 seconds.

traps.text: Giving every p the same subscript looks like numbering, but p1 is then assigned twice. It is only a renaming of p to p1, so the single assignment property is lost.
The left-hand sides are distinct, which looks like SSA, but the right-hand side names p2, p4 and q3 are never defined. SSA also requires every use to name its reaching definition.
Unnumbered uses of p and q on the right cannot be matched to one definition once p and q have several.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the static single assignment form of straight-line three address code in which p and q are each assigned twice, and the options differ only in subscripts.
recognize.contrast: Plain variable renaming only attaches a subscript; SSA also needs a distinct name per definition and, at a join point, a phi function. Here there are no branches, so only uniqueness and correct reaching names matter.

check.body: Run both programs on sample values a = 5, b = 2, c = 3, u = 2, v = 4. The original gives p = 3, q = 9, then p = 8, then q = 8 + 9 = 17. Option B gives p3 = 3, q4 = 9, p4 = 8, q5 = p4 + q4 = 8 + 9 = 17, the same final q. Option C cannot be run at all: q3 and p4 are read but never written.

hints.text: Look at what a variable name may do in single assignment form. How many statements can define one name, and what must each use read?
Static single assignment gives each assignment its own fresh name, so every name has exactly one definition in the program text.
After renaming, each use must carry the name of the definition that reaches it, which in straight-line code is the nearest assignment above it.
Write the original four statements beside each option and compare them one statement at a time, noting which names are new and which are reused.
Line 1 defines p and line 2 defines q, so those two names are taken; line 3 defines p again and must get a fresh name of its own.

variation.stem:
Consider the following three address code.

x = m + n
y = x * k
x = y - m
y = x + y

Which one of the following is a static single assignment form of this code?
variation.explanation: Give each of the four assignments a fresh name: x1, y1, x2, y2. Line 3 reads y from line 2, so y1. Line 4 reads x from line 3, which is x2, and y from line 2, which is y1. Option B reads the stale x1 in the last line, A reuses names, and D leaves the uses unnumbered.
